era: 1800 to October 2026; current claims checked October 14, 2026; confidence labels appear in facts

nodes.name: Second Great Awakening
nodes.summary: American revivals spread personal conversion, camp meetings, and lay preaching. Methodists and Baptists expanded, while new restoration and holiness movements emerged.
nodes.why: These revivals helped make conversion experiences and preaching central to American Protestant life alongside baptism and Communion.
facts: The revival began in the 1790s. Dates vary by region.
Barton Stone hosted the Cane Ridge camp meeting in Kentucky in 1801.
Presbyterian, Methodist, and Baptist preachers participated.
Early camp meetings grew from Presbyterian Communion gatherings.

nodes.name: African Methodist Episcopal Church
nodes.summary: Richard Allen united Black Methodist congregations in Philadelphia after racial discrimination in white churches. The AME Church joined Christian worship with education and freedom struggles.
nodes.why: Black Methodists formed their own churches to protect their dignity, leadership, and freedom.
facts: Mother Bethel began in 1794. The denomination organized in 1816.
Allen became its first bishop.
AME congregations supported abolition, schools, and civil rights.
WCC lists about 2.5M members without a census year. Current-size confidence low.
nodes.sacraments: Two sacraments, baptism and the Lord's Supper. The church baptizes infants. Believers receive Christ spiritually in Communion through faith, following Methodist teaching.
nodes.today: Roughly 2.5M reported. United States, Africa, and Caribbean.

nodes.name: Latter-day Saints
nodes.summary: Joseph Smith organized a church in New York claiming restored apostolic authority. Its scriptures, priesthood, and understanding of the Godhead differ from Nicene Christianity.
nodes.why: Churches use words such as baptism, sacrament, and restoration for different beliefs about God and church authority.
facts: Smith organized the church on April 6, 1830.
Its largest body is the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints.
Father, Son, and Holy Ghost are distinct beings united in purpose.
2025 registered membership was 17.9M. Confidence high for the church's reported count.
nodes.sacraments: Ordinances have no fixed sacrament count. Baptism uses immersion from age eight. Weekly bread and water remember Christ and renew covenants. Temples have additional ordinances.
nodes.today: LDS church reports 17.9M in 2025. Americas and worldwide.
nodes.disputed: Parents represent Smith's religious environment. Saints identify as Christian. Nicene churches reject their Godhead doctrine.

nodes.name: Stone-Campbell churches
nodes.summary: Barton Stone's and Alexander Campbell's movements united around 1832 to restore New Testament Christianity and Christian unity. Later divisions produced Churches of Christ, Christian Churches, and Disciples.
nodes.why: Weekly Communion and believers' baptism can accompany a strong rejection of denominational creeds and centralized authority.
facts: Stone's movement began in 1804. Campbell's organized reform began in 1809.
Churches of Christ became a separate US census category in 1906.
Disciples of Christ organized their present denominational structure in 1968.
Several million worldwide is a broad estimate. Confidence low without uniform membership counts.
nodes.sacraments: Baptism and Communion are ordinances or sacraments. Believers' immersion commonly relates to forgiveness. Weekly Communion generally commemorates Christ. Disciples also emphasize Christ's presence.
nodes.today: Several million worldwide. Strongest in United States and Africa.
nodes.disputed: Many Churches of Christ reject denominational labels. The branches differ over instruments, church cooperation, and how baptism relates to salvation.

nodes.name: Oxford Movement
nodes.summary: John Keble, John Henry Newman, and Edward Pusey defended Anglican continuity with the ancient church. Their teaching helped shape Anglo-Catholic worship and sacramental practice.
nodes.why: Its teaching helped give some Anglican churches Catholic forms of worship and a strong emphasis on sacramental grace.
facts: Tracts for the Times appeared from 1833 to 1841.
Tractarians emphasized bishops, apostolic succession, and the early church.
Newman joined the Roman Catholic Church in 1845.
Anglo-Catholic influence continued after the original movement.
nodes.sacraments: The movement renewed Anglican teaching on baptismal regeneration and Christ's real presence. It promoted confirmation, frequent Communion, and Eucharistic sacrifice.

nodes.name: Holiness churches
nodes.summary: Wesleyan Christians taught entire sanctification, God's grace enabling holy love and living. Phoebe Palmer's meetings spread the movement beyond Methodist institutions.
nodes.why: Methodist teaching about holiness shaped later revival churches and Pentecostal beliefs about spiritual experiences after conversion.
facts: The movement developed in the 1830s. 1837 marks Palmer's leadership of the Tuesday meetings.
Entire sanctification concerns devotion and freedom from sin's rule, not immunity from mistakes.
The Church of the Nazarene united holiness groups in 1907 and 1908.
Nazarenes report 2.76M members in 2025. Confidence high for that denomination, low for family totals.
nodes.sacraments: Usually two sacraments or ordinances. Baptism practices vary. Wesleyan churches treat Communion as a means of grace. The Salvation Army omits outward sacraments.
nodes.today: Millions worldwide. Nazarenes alone about 2.8M in 2025.

nodes.name: Great Disappointment
nodes.summary: Followers of Baptist preacher William Miller expected Christ's return on October 22, 1844. The failed expectation divided the movement and shaped several Adventist churches.
nodes.why: Adventist churches grew from an American revival movement, then developed different explanations of prophecy and Christian practice.
facts: Miller first expected the return in 1843 or 1844.
Samuel Snow promoted the October 22 date.
Sabbatarian Adventists later interpreted the date as a heavenly event.
Other Adventists rejected that interpretation.

nodes.name: Southern Baptist Convention
nodes.summary: Southern Baptists formed a convention in Augusta, Georgia, after disputes over appointing slaveholders as missionaries. The split defended slavery. Both sides retained Baptist beliefs about baptism and Communion.
nodes.why: Church divisions sometimes follow racial and political conflicts while preserving almost identical baptism and Communion practices.
facts: The convention formed in 1845.
Its founders defended slaveholding against restrictions by national Baptist mission boards.
The convention apologized for supporting slavery and racism in 1995.
2025 membership was 12.33M. Confidence high for the Annual Church Profile's reported total.
nodes.sacraments: Two ordinances. Believers' baptism by immersion publicly expresses faith. Bread and cup symbolically remember Christ's death. Local churches decide who may participate.
nodes.today: 12.3M reported members in 2025. Chiefly United States.

nodes.name: Adventist churches
nodes.summary: Several churches grew from Millerite expectations of Christ's return. Seventh-day Adventists organized in 1863, teaching Saturday Sabbath observance, Christ's return, and health reform.
nodes.why: Seventh-day Adventists share second-advent roots with other movements, including Jehovah's Witnesses, but teach different beliefs about God and Christian practice.
facts: Seventh-day Adventists formed their General Conference in May 1863.
Ellen White influenced their teaching and institutions.
The present Seventh-day Adventist Church explicitly teaches the Trinity.
SDA reported 23.68M baptized members at year-end 2024. Confidence high for its reported count.
nodes.sacraments: Seventh-day Adventists practice believers' immersion baptism and Communion as ordinances. Bread and grape juice symbolize Christ's body and blood. Foot washing precedes Communion.
nodes.today: SDA alone 23.7M members in 2024. Worldwide, especially Global South.
nodes.disputed: This branch covers broader Adventist origins. The sacramental and population details describe Seventh-day Adventists.

nodes.name: Salvation Army
nodes.summary: William and Catherine Booth's London mission combined evangelical preaching with practical help for poor people. It became the Salvation Army in 1878 and discontinued outward sacraments.
nodes.why: A Christian church can affirm grace and holy living while choosing to practice neither water baptism nor Communion.
facts: The Booths began the Christian Mission in London's East End in 1865.
The mission adopted the name Salvation Army in 1878.
It stopped administering baptism and Communion in 1883.
Its 2025 report lists 1.26M senior soldiers. Confidence high for that membership category.
nodes.sacraments: No outward sacraments. Salvationists practice neither water baptism nor bread-and-cup Communion. They emphasize inward grace, Christ's presence, and holiness in everyday life.
nodes.today: About 1.3M senior soldiers. Work spans 134 countries and territories.

nodes.name: Vatican I
nodes.summary: Pope Pius IX's council defined papal jurisdiction and infallibility for formal definitions of faith or morals addressed to the whole church. Opponents formed Old Catholic churches.
nodes.why: The council defined the pope's teaching authority. Some Catholics rejected that authority and formed separate churches while keeping seven sacraments.
facts: The council opened in December 1869.
Pastor Aeternus defined papal infallibility on July 18, 1870.
Infallibility concerns defined teaching, not every papal statement or personal conduct.
War and Rome's capture interrupted the council in 1870.
nodes.disputed: Catholics call the definition a development of apostolic teaching. Old Catholics, Orthodox, and Protestants reject the claimed authority.

nodes.name: Old Catholic churches
nodes.summary: German, Swiss, and Austrian Catholics who rejected Vatican I organized separate churches. They joined the older Utrecht church in a communion retaining bishops and seven sacraments.
nodes.why: Rejecting papal infallibility did not require abandoning Catholic sacramental worship or apostolic succession.
facts: Utrecht's separate episcopal history dates to 1723 and 1724.
The Union of Utrecht formed in 1889.
Old Catholics entered full communion with Anglicans in 1931.
WCC's roughly 115,000 figure lacks a census year. Current-size confidence low.
nodes.sacraments: Seven sacraments. Churches baptize infants and teach Christ's true presence in the Eucharist. They retain apostolic succession without requiring Rome's definition of transubstantiation.
nodes.today: Roughly 115,000 in Utrecht communion. Chiefly continental Europe. Estimate dated.
nodes.disputed: Many independent groups call themselves Old Catholic. This node describes the historic Utrecht communion.

nodes.name: Orthodox national churches
nodes.summary: Eastern Orthodox churches formed self-governing national bodies. Disputes over territory and ethnic boundaries sometimes interrupted communion while the churches retained shared sacramental doctrines.
nodes.why: Autocephaly lets an Orthodox church govern itself while retaining Orthodox beliefs and sacraments.
facts: Moscow's patriarchate dates to 1589, before this era.
Constantinople's 1872 council condemned ethnic church organization and declared the Bulgarian hierarchy schismatic.
Not every Orthodox church accepted that judgment.
Constantinople recognized Bulgarian autocephaly and ended the schism in 1945.
nodes.disputed: Orthodox churches disagree over who may grant autocephaly and how territorial boundaries should operate.

nodes.name: Jehovah's Witnesses
nodes.summary: Charles Taze Russell's Bible study movement developed in the 1870s. Its main successor adopted the name Jehovah's Witnesses in 1931 and rejects Nicene teaching about God.
nodes.why: Their baptism and annual remembrance of Jesus differ from the theology and Communion practice of Nicene churches.
facts: Russell began publishing Zion's Watch Tower in 1879.
Witnesses teach that Jesus is God's first creation and the Spirit is God's active force.
Most attend the annual Memorial without eating its bread or drinking its wine.
2025 peak active publishers numbered 9.21M. Confidence high for the reported category.
nodes.sacraments: Immersion baptism dedicates believers to Jehovah. The annual Memorial uses symbolic bread and wine. Only those claiming heavenly anointing partake. Witnesses have no seven-sacrament system.
nodes.today: About 9.2M peak active publishers in 2025. Worldwide.
nodes.disputed: The Adventist parent represents second-advent influences. Witnesses identify as Christian. Nicene churches reject their doctrine of Christ.

nodes.name: National Baptist Convention
nodes.summary: Black Baptist organizations united in Atlanta in 1895 for missions, education, and publishing. Their churches sustained Black leadership and later supplied major civil rights leaders.
nodes.why: Black Baptist churches preserved Baptist ordinances while building institutions beyond white control.
facts: Three national Black Baptist organizations merged in 1895.
Later divisions produced several National Baptist conventions.
Martin Luther King Jr. worked within this tradition before the Progressive National Baptist split.
Self-reports and religious censuses differ. Confidence low for a precise current membership total.
nodes.sacraments: Two ordinances. Believers' immersion publicly confesses faith. The Lord's Supper remembers Christ with symbolic bread and cup. Congregations decide who may participate.
nodes.today: Several million, chiefly African American congregations in United States.

nodes.name: Pentecostal churches
nodes.summary: William Seymour's Azusa Street revival spread Pentecostal worship internationally. Pentecostals emphasize the Holy Spirit's power, healing, and spiritual gifts, including speaking in tongues.
nodes.why: Most Pentecostal churches practice water baptism and Communion. They also teach Spirit baptism as a distinct experience of spiritual power.
facts: Azusa Street began in Los Angeles in 1906. Interracial worship marked its early years.
Earlier roots include Charles Parham's Topeka school in 1901.
The Assemblies of God organized in Hot Springs, Arkansas, in 1914.
2026 Pentecostal-charismatic total is about 676M across churches. Confidence medium. The categories overlap.
nodes.sacraments: Usually two ordinances, believers' immersion and symbolic Communion. Spirit baptism is a distinct experience of spiritual power. Some churches also practice foot washing.
nodes.today: Hundreds of millions worldwide. Especially Africa, Latin America, and Asia.
nodes.disputed: 1906 marks international expansion. Pentecostals had earlier roots. Most are Trinitarian. Oneness churches appear separately.

nodes.name: Edinburgh missionary conference
nodes.summary: Protestant and Anglican mission leaders met in Edinburgh to coordinate evangelism. Their cooperation helped launch the modern ecumenical movement and later interchurch organizations.
nodes.why: Churches began seeking practical cooperation and visible unity without first settling every doctrinal or sacramental disagreement.
facts: Most delegates came from Western Protestant mission agencies.
Catholic and Orthodox churches did not participate as partner churches.
The meeting created a continuation committee.
The conference helped prepare the way for the World Council of Churches.

nodes.name: Oneness Pentecostals
nodes.summary: Pentecostals who taught God's oneness and baptism in Jesus' name separated from Trinitarian colleagues. Their theology rejects the Nicene distinction of three eternal divine persons.
nodes.why: Baptism in Jesus' name expresses these churches' beliefs about God and salvation.
facts: The Jesus' name controversy began in 1913.
The Assemblies of God's Trinitarian statement prompted a major separation in 1916.
The United Pentecostal Church International formed in 1945.
UPCI reports 5.75M constituents in a 2024 release. Confidence medium. Other Oneness groups add more.
nodes.sacraments: Ordinances include baptism, Communion, and often foot washing. Immersion in Jesus' name relates to forgiveness. UPCI links salvation with Spirit baptism and tongues.
nodes.today: UPCI alone reports about 5.8M constituents worldwide. Broader total uncertain.
nodes.disputed: Oneness believers identify as Christian and reject the label modalist. Nicene churches reject their doctrine of divine persons.

nodes.name: Fundamentalist-modernist controversy
nodes.summary: American Protestants fought over biblical authority, miracles, and adapting theology to modern scholarship. The conflict divided denominations and helped distinguish later evangelical and mainline networks.
nodes.why: Disagreements over reading Scripture divided modern Protestants even when they shared beliefs about baptism and Communion.
facts: Harry Emerson Fosdick preached Shall the Fundamentalists Win? in 1922.
J. Gresham Machen argued that liberal Christianity changed the faith itself.
Machen helped establish Westminster Seminary in 1929.
The Orthodox Presbyterian Church formed in 1936.
nodes.disputed: Conservatives defended doctrinal continuity. Modernists sought credible Christian teaching alongside historical criticism and science. Neither camp represented all Protestants.

nodes.name: World Council of Churches
nodes.summary: Churches founded the World Council of Churches in Amsterdam as a fellowship for unity, witness, and service. Orthodox and Protestant churches cooperate without merging their denominations.
nodes.why: Ecumenical cooperation can include shared study of baptism and Eucharist while churches retain different sacramental rules.
facts: The first assembly brought together 147 member churches.
The WCC is a fellowship. Member churches retain their own authority.
The Catholic Church cooperates but is not a member.
Churches widely discussed its 1982 text Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry.

nodes.name: Independent evangelical churches
nodes.summary: Independent evangelical churches expanded through Bible teaching, conversion preaching, church planting, and contemporary worship. Some grew into megachurches, while others remained small congregations.
nodes.why: A church's lack of a denominational name does not imply a single theology of baptism or Communion.
facts: 1950 marks postwar growth, not the first independent church.
Megachurches commonly have at least 2,000 weekly worshippers and can also belong to denominations.
Pew found nondenominational Protestants were 7% of US adults in 2023-24. Confidence high for this survey.
Worldwide evangelical-independent totals lack one definition. Confidence low.
nodes.sacraments: Usually two ordinances, believers' baptism and symbolic Communion. Frequency varies. Some churches retain infant baptism or Christ's spiritual presence. Charismatic churches emphasize spiritual gifts.
nodes.today: Millions worldwide. Strongest in Americas, Africa, and Asia.
nodes.disputed: Parents represent common influences. Independent, evangelical, charismatic, and megachurch labels overlap, but each describes something different.

nodes.name: US mainline mergers
nodes.summary: American Protestant denominations reunited older branches or joined related traditions. These mergers created the UCC, United Methodist Church, PCUSA, and ELCA. Each retained its own sacramental tradition.
nodes.why: The family tree includes branches joining together as well as splitting apart.
facts: 1957 UCC joined Congregational Christian Churches with the Evangelical and Reformed Church.
1968 United Methodist Church joined Methodists with the Evangelical United Brethren.
1983 PCUSA reunited the Presbyterian Church in the US with the United Presbyterian Church in the USA.
1988 ELCA united the ALC, LCA, and Association of Evangelical Lutheran Churches.

nodes.name: Charismatic renewal
nodes.summary: Christians brought Pentecostal-style prayer, healing, and spiritual gifts into existing denominations. Protestant renewal gained attention in 1960. Catholic renewal spread from Duquesne University in 1967.
nodes.why: Spiritual gifts can coexist with Catholic, Anglican, Lutheran, or other established sacramental teaching.
facts: Episcopal priest Dennis Bennett publicized his experience of tongues in 1960.
The Duquesne Weekend helped begin Catholic charismatic renewal in February 1967.
Many participants stayed within their existing churches.
Charismatics share the 2026 combined 676M Pentecostal-charismatic estimate. Separate total uncertain. Confidence medium.
nodes.sacraments: Participants retain their churches' sacrament counts, baptism practices, and Eucharistic beliefs. Spirit baptism means spiritual renewal. Catholics do not count it as an additional sacrament.
nodes.today: Hundreds of millions across denominations worldwide. Counts overlap Pentecostals.
nodes.disputed: Participants belong to different denominations. The Pentecostal parent represents influence on their worship.

nodes.name: Vatican II
nodes.summary: The Catholic council renewed worship, encouraged lay participation, and committed Catholics to dialogue with other Christians. It permitted wider use of local languages. Later reforms changed the Mass.
nodes.why: The council allowed wider use of local languages in Catholic worship and encouraged dialogue with other Christians.
facts: John XXIII opened the council. Paul VI completed it.
Sacrosanctum Concilium authorized expanded vernacular use while preserving Latin in principle.
Unitatis Redintegratio addressed Christian unity in 1964.
The reformed Roman Missal followed in 1969 and 1970.
nodes.sacraments: The council retained seven sacraments, baptismal grace, transubstantiation, and Eucharistic sacrifice. It promoted active participation, Scripture readings, and approved liturgy in local languages.
nodes.disputed: Catholics dispute some later interpretations and reforms. The council itself did not abolish Latin or redefine the Eucharist as merely symbolic.

nodes.name: 1054 excommunications lifted
nodes.summary: Pope Paul VI and Patriarch Athenagoras removed the 1054 excommunications from church memory. Their joint declaration encouraged Catholic-Orthodox reconciliation. The churches remained divided.
nodes.why: Reconciliation gestures and theological dialogue can advance without making Catholic and Orthodox Communion interchangeable.
facts: The declaration appeared on December 7, 1965.
The original censures targeted particular people, not every member of both churches.
Both sides regretted the words and actions that deepened estrangement.
Lifting the censures did not end the schism or restore shared Eucharistic communion.

nodes.name: Joint declaration on justification
nodes.summary: The Lutheran World Federation and Catholic Church agreed on basic truths about justification by God's grace through faith. They judged earlier condemnations inapplicable to the agreed teaching.
nodes.why: A central Reformation disagreement narrowed, while differences about church authority, ministry, and sacraments remained.
facts: Representatives signed the declaration in Augsburg on October 31, 1999.
The agreement describes a consensus in basic truths, not identical theology on every point.
It did not create full church communion or general permission for shared Eucharist.
Some Lutheran churches outside the federation reject the agreement.
nodes.disputed: Supporters see doctrinal agreement. Critics argue that important differences remain or that the document weakens Lutheran teaching.

nodes.name: GAFCON Anglican realignment
nodes.summary: Conservative Anglican leaders organized GAFCON amid conflicts over sexuality and biblical authority. They supported ACNA and later claimed to reorganize global Anglican communion beyond Canterbury's institutions.
nodes.why: Anglican identity now depends on disputed relationships between provinces, shared doctrine, and Communion institutions.
facts: GAFCON met in Jerusalem and issued its declaration in 2008.
It supported ACNA's formation in 2009.
GAFCON announced its Global Anglican Communion initiative in October 2025.
The March 2026 Abuja Affirmation rejected Canterbury's governing instruments. Confidence high for GAFCON's stated position.
nodes.disputed: GAFCON claims to restore historic Anglican faith. Other Anglicans dispute its authority and its claim to speak for the Communion.

nodes.name: ACNA
nodes.summary: The Anglican Church in North America united conservative Anglican groups, including congregations leaving Episcopal and Canadian Anglican churches. Several overseas Anglican provinces recognized the new body.
nodes.why: An Anglican church can retain its liturgy and sacraments while changing which bishops and provinces it recognizes.
facts: ACNA formed in 2009.
Conflicts included sexuality, biblical authority, and episcopal oversight.
Recognition by overseas provinces does not equal membership in Canterbury's Anglican Communion institutions.
Its current official welcome page reports over 130,000 members. Confidence medium for this rounded claim.
nodes.sacraments: Two principal sacraments, baptism and Eucharist, plus five sacramental rites. Churches baptize infants. Eucharistic teaching ranges from Reformed spiritual presence to Anglo-Catholic real presence.
nodes.today: Over 130,000 reported members. United States, Canada, and Latin America.
nodes.disputed: ACNA calls itself an Anglican province. Its status within the wider Communion remains contested.

nodes.name: Moscow-Constantinople communion break
nodes.summary: Moscow ended Eucharistic communion with Constantinople over its decisions concerning Ukraine. The Orthodox Church of Ukraine's later independence deepened disputes over church boundaries and recognition.
nodes.why: Orthodox churches can share sacramental beliefs while refusing Eucharistic communion because they dispute who has authority over a territory.
facts: Moscow's Holy Synod announced the break on October 15, 2018.
Constantinople had moved toward Ukrainian autocephaly and restored previously excluded Ukrainian hierarchs.
The OCU formed in December 2018 and received its tomos in January 2019.
This was a jurisdictional rupture inside Orthodoxy, not a new creed or sacramental system.
nodes.sacraments: Both retain Orthodox baptism and Eucharistic real presence. Moscow forbids its clergy and faithful from receiving Communion in Constantinople's churches.
nodes.disputed: Moscow claims authority in Ukraine. Constantinople disputes that claim and asserts authority to grant church independence. Orthodox churches differ over recognition.

nodes.name: Orthodox Church of Ukraine
nodes.summary: A Kyiv council united Ukrainian Orthodox groups in December 2018. Patriarch Bartholomew granted the new church independence in January 2019. Moscow rejects that decision.
nodes.why: A self-governing Orthodox church retains Orthodox beliefs and sacraments. Disputes over its independence affect which churches share Communion with it.
facts: The unification council elected Metropolitan Epiphanius in December 2018.
Bartholomew signed the tomos on January 5 and presented it on January 6, 2019.
It is distinct from the Ukrainian Orthodox Church historically linked to Moscow.
Razumkov's 2024 survey found 35% identifying with OCU. Confidence medium. This is identification, not membership.
nodes.sacraments: Orthodox mysteries, commonly counted as seven. Infants receive baptism, chrismation, and Communion. The church teaches Eucharistic real presence. Church independence concerns governance.
nodes.today: Millions identify with OCU in Ukraine. Exact membership uncertain.
nodes.disputed: Constantinople recognizes its autocephaly. Moscow rejects it. Orthodox recognition is partial, so communion depends on the particular church.

nodes.name: United Methodist split
nodes.summary: Disputes over sexuality, biblical authority, and enforcing church rules led thousands of congregations to leave the United Methodist Church. Many joined the Global Methodist Church.
nodes.why: Both churches kept Methodist sacraments. The split chiefly changed church affiliation and rules about marriage and ordination.
facts: The 2019 General Conference strengthened restrictions and authorized a temporary US disaffiliation process.
The Global Methodist Church launched on May 1, 2022.
About 7,600 US congregations left in 2019-2023. Not all joined the GMC.
UMC removed bans on gay clergy and same-sex weddings in 2024. Confidence high.
nodes.disputed: Conservatives emphasize biblical authority and continuity. Supporters of inclusion emphasize equal participation. Departing congregations chose several destinations.

nodes.name: Global Methodist Church
nodes.summary: Conservative Methodists formed a new denomination as United Methodist divisions widened. The Global Methodist Church retains Wesleyan theology and teaches marriage between a man and a woman.
nodes.why: Its doctrinal separation concerns authority and sexual ethics more than baptism or Eucharistic presence.
facts: The denomination launched on May 1, 2022.
Its convening General Conference met in Costa Rica in September 2024.
Its doctrine retains infant baptism and two sacraments as means of grace.
The church reported 7,250 congregations in September 2026. No global adherent total accompanies that report.
Its next General Conference met in Johannesburg, South Africa, in 2026.
nodes.sacraments: Two sacraments, infant or adult baptism and Holy Communion. Communion conveys grace and Christ's body and blood spiritually through faith. Bread and wine remain unchanged.
nodes.today: 7,250 congregations reported in September 2026. Global adherent total unverified.

nodes.name: Global South growth
nodes.summary: Christian populations grew in Africa, Latin America, and Asia. Africa now has the largest continental Christian population. Europe has lost its former numerical dominance.
nodes.why: Growing churches in Africa, Latin America, and Asia shape Christian worship, mission, and debates worldwide.
facts: Pew's 2025 study places 31% of 2020 Christians in sub-Saharan Africa, ahead of every other region.
The 2026 World Christian Database estimates about 780M Christians in Africa, the largest continent.
It estimates 69% of Christians live in the Global South in 2026.
Confidence high for Africa's leading position. Medium for current modeled population estimates.
nodes.disputed: Pew measures religious identification. Church databases use broader affiliation and estimates. Their absolute totals differ, but both show Africa's growth.

nodes.name: Nicaea 1700th anniversary
nodes.summary: Pope Leo XIV, Patriarch Bartholomew, and other Christian leaders prayed at Iznik on November 28, 2025. They commemorated 1,700 years since the first Council of Nicaea.
nodes.why: The Nicene faith remains shared across major Christian traditions even where church government and Eucharistic communion remain divided.
facts: Iznik in Türkiye is ancient Nicaea, the council's meeting place in 325.
Leaders gathered near the archaeological remains of Saint Neophytos Basilica.
They commemorated shared faith and prayed for Christian unity.
Vatican and independent reports confirm the completed November 2025 gathering. Confidence high.

nodes.name: Christianity today
nodes.summary: Catholic, Protestant, independent, Eastern Orthodox, and Oriental Orthodox churches remain distinct in October 2026. Counts differ by membership definitions, reference year, and how researchers count overlapping movements.
nodes.why: These figures give an approximate sense of size. Membership totals do not measure agreement about Christian beliefs.
facts: The Vatican reports 1.422B baptized Catholics for 2024.
WCD estimates 1.06B Protestants and independents in 2026, including Pentecostal churches.
WCD estimates 293M Orthodox Christians in 2026, combining Eastern and Oriental churches.
Pentecostal and charismatic counts overlap denominations. These totals use different sources and cannot form a consistent global sum.
nodes.disputed: The Vatican counts baptized Catholics. WCD uses different definitions. Subtracting totals from different sources cannot reliably count Eastern Orthodox.
